results.authors: Fischer U, Koga M, Strbian D, et al.
results.key_finding: Early DOAC initiation (within 48 hours after a minor or moderate stroke, on day 6 or 7 after a major stroke, by imaging size) had a 30-day composite of recurrent ischaemic stroke, systemic embolism, major bleeding, symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage or vascular death of 2.9% versus 4.1% with later initiation; symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage occurred in 0.2% in both groups.
results.title: Early versus Later Anticoagulation for Stroke with Atrial Fibrillation (ELAN)

results.authors: Werring DJ, Dehbi HM, Ahmed N, et al.
results.key_finding: DOAC initiation within 4 days of onset was non-inferior to delayed initiation at 7 to 14 days for recurrent stroke, symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage, unclassifiable stroke or systemic embolism at 90 days.
results.title: Optimal timing of anticoagulation after acute ischaemic stroke with atrial fibrillation (OPTIMAS)

results.authors: Dawson J, Bejot Y, Christensen LM, et al.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give IV thrombolysis before non-contrast CT excludes intracranial haemorrhage.
Do not give IV thrombolysis while blood pressure is 185/110 mmHg or higher.
Do not give IV thrombolysis if INR is above 1.7, the platelet count is below 100,000, there was recent major surgery, or another guideline-listed contraindication is present.
Do not delay non-contrast CT for additional imaging or laboratory results in a stroke alert.
Do not delay thrombectomy to observe the response to IV thrombolysis.
Do not start anticoagulation within 24 hours of IV thrombolysis or before follow-up imaging excludes haemorrhagic transformation, and do not bridge with heparin.
Do not leave her on antiplatelet therapy alone or without anticoagulation because of the nosebleeds.
Do not restart warfarin when a DOAC is suitable.
required_recommendations: Establish last known well (09:00, 2 hours 22 minutes before arrival) and the NIHSS (19).

IV thrombolysis: give once blood pressure is below 185/110 mmHg (2 hours 22 minutes from last known well; warfarin stopped 3 weeks ago, INR 1.1; platelets 259; no active bleeding, and past nosebleeds are not a contraindication). Thrombectomy: proceed for the left M1 occlusion (NIHSS 19, living independently before the stroke, ASPECTS 10, within 6 hours); do not wait for the response to thrombolysis.
Achieve a door-to-needle time under 60 minutes.

Lower blood pressure below 185/110 mmHg (196/111 on arrival) with IV labetalol or nicardipine before IV thrombolysis, then keep it below 180/105 mmHg for 24 hours; after successful recanalization do not target systolic blood pressure below 140 mmHg.
Admit to a stroke unit with continuous cardiac monitoring (telemetry) for at least the first 24 hours.

Control the ventricular rate of atrial fibrillation (104 to 108 bpm on arrival, above 120 bpm for 3.2 hours on monitoring; she takes no rate-control medicine) with a beta-blocker, avoiding hypotension.

Repeat troponin and review the ECG; the mild elevation (troponin I 0.05 ng/mL) is most likely demand ischaemia from rapid atrial fibrillation or neurogenic myocardial injury; it does not delay reperfusion.
Treat hyperglycaemia (glucose 205 mg/dL) to 140 to 180 mg/dL during the first 24 hours, avoiding hypoglycaemia with her glipizide.

Start apixaban 5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation (CHA2DS2-VASc 9; HAS-BLED 4 for uncontrolled hypertension, this stroke, bleeding history and age over 65) on day 6 to 7, because the infarct is major by ELAN imaging criteria (frontal, parietal and insular cortex, more than one cortical MCA branch), once follow-up imaging excludes haemorrhagic transformation; do not bridge with heparin.

Treat the bleeding source so that anticoagulation can continue: ENT assessment of the recurrent epistaxis, iron studies for the microcytosis (MCV 79), and long-term blood pressure control; reserve left atrial appendage occlusion for anticoagulation that proves impossible.
Discuss with her and her daughter why anticoagulation must continue despite the nosebleeds, and that a DOAC carries a lower intracranial bleeding risk than warfarin.
Intensify lipid lowering (LDL 136 mg/dL on rosuvastatin 20 mg) to an LDL below 70 mg/dL, with rosuvastatin 40 mg or added ezetimibe, for aortic and carotid atherosclerosis and diabetes.

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Jing Li is a 78-year-old right-handed East Asian woman with a history of atrial fibrillation (recently self-discontinued warfarin three weeks ago due to recurrent epistaxis), poorly controlled hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction who was brought to the emergency department by EMS after an acute onset of right-sided weakness and speech difficulty. Her daughter reports that she spoke with her mother on the phone at approximately 09:00 this morning and she was completely normal, discussing plans for a family dinner this weekend. At approximately 10:45, a neighbor found Mrs. Jing Li on the floor of her kitchen, awake but unable to speak coherently and with her right arm and leg limp. The neighbor called 911 immediately. EMS arrived at 10:58 and documented left gaze preference, dense right hemiplegia, and expressive aphasia. A stroke alert was activated in the field. Prehospital finger-stick glucose was 204 mg/dL. The patient was transported emergently to the nearest comprehensive stroke center, arriving at 11:22. On arrival, telemetry immediately demonstrated an irregularly irregular rhythm consistent with atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 108 bpm. The patient was visibly anxious and attempting to speak but producing only fragmentary, effortful words. She was able to follow simple one-step commands with her left hand. Her daughter arrived shortly after and confirmed that her mother had stopped taking warfarin approximately three weeks ago because she was having frequent nosebleeds and was afraid of 'bleeding out.' She had not yet seen her cardiologist to discuss alternative anticoagulation. The daughter also notes her mother's blood pressure has been running high at home despite medications, with readings in the 170s-180s systolic. There was no preceding headache, seizure, recent trauma, fever, or change in baseline function prior to today's event. Last known well time is established at 09:00, approximately 2 hours and 22 minutes prior to ED arrival.
